items.title: U.S. embassy accuses Canadian politicians of interfering in American elections
items.description: The U.S. embassy in Canada has released a list of quotes from Canadian politicians which it says indicate 'plans to influence American politics.'
items._ogDesc: The U.S. embassy in Canada has released a list of quotes from Canadian politicians which it says indicate 'plans to influence American politics.'
items.body:
OTTAWA — Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford both disputed the suggestion of Canadian interference in the U.S. midterms, after the U.S. embassy in Canada released a list of quotes from Canadian politicians which it claims indicate “plans to influence American politics.”

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly is quoted five times in the list the embassy released Wednesday.

It includes quotes offered without context about pressuring American businesses and targeting U.S. states through counter-tariffs. Joly made the comments while addressing Canada’s response to U.S.-imposed tariffs.

The Canadian Press asked for comment from Joly but she was not made available.

In a news conference on Parliament Hill Wednesday, Carney — flanked by Joly — responded to a question about the U.S. list by pointing out that the United States initiated trade actions against Canada.

“All of our actions are in the interests of Canadian workers, Canadian families and the future of this economy,” Carney told reporters after announcing a $9 billion aid package in response to U.S. tariffs.

Ford, who is also quoted in the U.S. embassy release, said he has “no interest at all” in interfering in American elections.

“I’ll tell you what the American people want. They want certainty, they want stability,” Ford said, noting he spent 20 years in the United States and “loves the American people.”

“We’re going to focus on what we can do here in Ontario and in Canada to make sure we protect our economy, protect the people and protect communities. That’s what we’re going to focus on, and the people of the United States will make that determination in the midterms.”

Americans head to the polls on Nov. 3 for midterm elections that could end Republican control over Congress.

U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra said earlier this month American officials are “closely watching” Canadian politicians for signs of election interference.

During an interview on The Really Big Show podcast released on Oct. 14, Hoekstra said political ads run by the province of Ontario last year could be interpreted as political interference.

U.S. President Donald Trump ended trade talks with Canada in October 2025 after Ontario aired an ad during the World Series using clips of former U.S. president Ronald Reagan criticizing tariffs and supporting free trade.

Hoekstra also cited recent comments by Joly and former prime minister Justin Trudeau and suggested they also could amount to interference.

Hoekstra went on to warn Canadian politicians to keep their “nose out” of American politics in the weeks before the midterm elections.

Trudeau criticized the Trump administration during a discussion at Brown University on Sept. 22.

“There is a pattern here of doing things that are driving up prices for your consumers and not necessarily making anything better for America, by fighting with one of your oldest and best allies,” Trudeau said during the event.

In the interview, Hoekstra said Joly made comments about targeting retaliatory tariffs at “politically sensitive states.”

Joly pushed back last week, telling reporters Canada would never engage in election interference and would “never accept that also being done to us in Canada.”

Joly said she has been to the U.S. in recent months and has met with Democrats and Republicans.

“Fundamentally, what I’ve done in the U.S. is to attract investments,” she said. “I think I’ll be able to have good news of investments by different American companies to Canada. And that’s exactly what I’m doing and that will continue to be my strategy in the U.S. and also around the world.”

Hoekstra said if any actions by Canadians end up amounting to election interference, the United States will respond.

Wednesday’s post from the embassy ended by saying “Americans decide America’s elections.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 21, 2026.

With files from Nick Murray and Catherine Morrison

items._ogDesc: Some government websites have been taken down temporarily as a precaution against a security risk, says Artificial Intelligence Minister Evan Solomon.
items.body:
OTTAWA — Some government websites have been taken down temporarily as a precaution against a security risk, Artificial Intelligence Minister Evan Solomon said Wednesday.

In a social media post, Solomon said the websites went dark to protect government systems and Canadians’ information following guidance from the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security.

He said it is being done in response to a vulnerability identified in PHP, a widely used programming language.

“This is a global issue, and other governments and organizations are also taking protective measures,” he said.

The website of the Finnish government was only partly available Wednesday. A message to visitors said Finnish government websites were experiencing a temporary disruption and were fully or partially unavailable while the issue was being resolved.

The FBI’s cyber division said the vulnerability could allow malicious actors to remotely execute code in the programming language, potentially compromising sensitive data and networks.

The PHP Foundation, which includes developers who work on securing the programming language, said it has released fixes for the vulnerabilities, along with instructions on how to update systems.

Solomon said affected federal websites will be restored once patches are applied. The Canadian Press has asked Treasury Board which government websites have been taken down but has not yet received a response.

“We take this situation extremely seriously,” said Solomon. “Thank you to the cybersecurity teams working to protect the services Canadians rely on.”

The British Columbia government posted Wednesday on social media that it had taken some of its webpages offline “as a precaution following a new global cybersecurity vulnerability.”

It is unclear if it is the same risk as the one the federal government announced, but the B.C. government said teams were working to restore services as soon as possible.

items.title: Tesla cuts spending before potential SpaceX deal even as Musk bets future on AI, robots
items.description: Tesla cut its annual capital expenditure forecast by a fifth and posted positive free cash flow in the third quarter, after investing far less in its AI and robotics ambitions than expected.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Elon Musk attends the annual meeting of the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, Jan. 22, 2026. (AP Photo/Markus Schreiber, File)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Markus Schreiber</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Tesla cut its annual capital expenditure forecast by a fifth and posted positive free cash flow in the third quarter, after investing far less in its AI and robotics ambitions than expected.
items.body:
Tesla cut its annual capital expenditure forecast by a fifth and posted surprise positive free cash flow in the third quarter on Wednesday, after investing far less in its AI and robotics ambitions than Wall Street had expected.

The unexpected cash generated in the quarter comes at a critical moment for Tesla, as CEO Elon Musk explores combining the EV maker with his far more capital-intensive space venture, SpaceX.

While the lower spending strengthens Tesla’s financial position ahead of any deal, preserving cash at the expense of investment — in AI, robotaxis and humanoid robots — could undermine the very growth story investors are betting on.

  • Latest updates on company news here

Tesla shares, which had risen two per cent in after-hours trading after the company reported positive cash flow, higher gross margin and market-beating revenue, reversed course to trade down two per cent. They have fallen about 14 per cent this year.

“The free cash flow beat was a pleasant surprise, but when combined with the lower-than-expected capex, raises questions on the next step for the automaker,” said Ryan Lee, senior vice president of product and strategy at Direxion, which offers ETFs tied to Tesla. “Lower capex suggests less of an ‘all-in’ approach to the AI arms race than one would expect from Elon.”

Tesla said it expected capital expenses for 2026 to be roughly US$20 billion, down from its previous forecast of more than US$25 billion, but did not say what it would spend less on.

In the third quarter ended September 30, Tesla spent US$4.7 billion in capex, double that of a year ago, but lower than the US$7.5 billion analysts on average were expecting, according to LSEG data. Tesla reported free cash flow of US$1.53 billion, compared with an expected US$4.92 billion cash burn.

SpaceX merger under discussion

Musk said on Tuesday that a merger between Tesla and SpaceX was a “good idea” and that the companies had formed special committees to discuss a deal. On Wednesday, Musk said on a conference call with analysts that he had no more to say on the matter.

A merger would create a single company at the center of Musk’s long-term vision: an integrated technology and manufacturing empire spanning AI, energy, robotics, communications and transportation on Earth and beyond.

Still, investors will seek evidence that Tesla is investing enough to turn Musk’s ambitions into commercial businesses, with the robotaxi rollout lagging his promises. Tesla’s energy unit has recently offered a counterweight to its auto business, which remains under scrutiny as rivals globally launch newer, often cheaper models. Tesla still leans heavily on the aging Model 3 and Model Y.

“The merger still faces a high bar, but tonight’s numbers make the financial logic harder to ignore,” said Thomas Monteiro, a senior analyst at Investing.com.

“The main takeaway is that Tesla’s surprisingly positive cash flow quarter did not come from stronger profits, but from spending billions less than planned at a time when SpaceX is preparing to invest up to $40 billion in a single quarter.”

Revenue flat but beats estimates

Revenue was flat from a year earlier, despite the end of US tax credits that supported sales last year. That was enough to top Wall Street targets. Net income plunged 43 per cent.

Tesla said in a statement that it ended the quarter with the largest backlog for its passenger vehicles in four years. High gasoline prices have stoked demand for EVs, especially in Europe.

With 486,532 vehicles delivered in the third quarter, Tesla is on track to increase annual deliveries for the first time in three years.

  • Latest technology news on BNNBloomberg.ca

“Demand is growing rapidly for our vehicles. It’s exceeding our production by a significant margin,” Musk said on the conference call with analysts. “In a nutshell, after many years of sort of grind and things being fairly flat, I think we’re now headed for a lot of fun and significant growth.”

The FSD (supervised) attach rate reached over three-quarters of new vehicle deliveries in North America, a nearly 20-percentage-point increase from the second quarter, Tesla said.

Automotive gross margin, excluding regulatory credits, came in at 18.1 per cent in the third quarter, higher than analysts’ estimates of 16.7 per cent, according to Visible Alpha data.

Tesla said it was aiming to produce five million vehicles a year by about 2030, up from an expected 2.5 million this year.

Reporting by Akash Sriram in Bengaluru and Abhirup Roy in San Francisco; Additional reporting by Chris Kirkham in Los Angeles; Writing by Sayantani Ghosh; Editing by Pooja Desai, Peter Henderson and Matthew Lewis

items._ogDesc: Companies controlled by billionaire B.C. property developer Terry Hui allege that the Canada Revenue Agency has engaged in a “pattern of misconduct” in its attempts to collect on ballooning tax debts dating as far back as 2007.
items.body:
Companies controlled by billionaire B.C. property developer Terry Hui allege that the Canada Revenue Agency has engaged in a “pattern of misconduct” in its attempts to collect on ballooning tax debts dating as far back as 2007.

Five companies within Hui’s real estate development group are targeted in the audit by the CRA, including Adex Securities, One West Holdings, a B.C. numbered company and two Luxembourg-based shell companies.

The companies filed an application in Federal Court this month, claiming the government has wrongfully moved to collect on tax debts totalling nearly $330 million, most of which is accrued interest.

The application says the group is involved in capital-intensive real estate projects in Toronto, Vancouver and Calgary and the audit, initiated in 2013, focused on transactions that relied on Canada’s tax treaty with Luxembourg.

The companies say in the application that they’ve received tax debt assessments this year, with Adex owing $45 million and interest of more than $65 million, while the two Luxembourg-based companies owe together more than $92 million and $127 million in interest.

They want the court to stop the government from collecting on the debts until a related case filed earlier this year is concluded, while objecting to the CRA wanting $115 million security payment from Adex.

Requiring a payment that large and not allowing the company to defer will cause the real estate group to “lose significant capital that is currently being used to fund active development projects.”

The application is one of at least three filed in Federal Court this year related to the dispute, where they claim that being forced to pay will cause “irreparable harm” and that no advance notice from the CRA means that they “could not have reasonably planned for a debt … of this magnitude.”

The companies claim the revenue agency has exhibited a “pattern of misconduct,” alleging its officers acted outside established policies and procedures and “without regard to the impact of their actions on taxpayer businesses.”

Lawyers for the companies were not immediately available for comment, but Justin Kutyan with KPMG Law in Toronto told The Canadian Press earlier this year that the transactions in the case were similar to a tax structure upheld by the Supreme Court of Canada in 2021.

The court ruled 6-3 in favour of Alta Energy Luxembourg, which had claimed a tax exemption on a capital gain of more than $380 million under Canada’s treaty with Luxembourg, described in the decision as being “well known as an international tax haven.”

The court found in Alta’s favour, ruling that Canadian tax authorities couldn’t use anti-tax avoidance rules to “judicially amend or renegotiate a treaty.”

The dissenting justices in the case, however, said “the federal government did not deliberately set out to create the conditions for unlimited tax avoidance by means of schemes” used by the company.

The dissenters wrote that “the court should not legitimize such blatantly abusive tax avoidance based on the view that Canada should have negotiated different treaty terms.”

The CRA said it did not have a spokesperson available for an interview to comment on tax treaty abuse.

This report by Darryl Greer of The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 21, 2026.

items.title: ‘Alarm and concern’: Canada’s Armenian population reacts to PM’s trip to Türkiye
items.description: Mark Carney’s trip to Türkiye Wednesday marks the first ever bilateral visit to the country by a Canadian prime minister.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Prime Minister Mark Carney meets with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan in Ankara, Turkey, Tuesday, July 7, 2026. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Adrian Wyld]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu"></media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Mark Carney’s trip to Türkiye Wednesday marks the first ever bilateral visit to the country by a Canadian prime minister.
items.body:
Mark Carney’s trip to Türkiye Wednesday marks the first ever bilateral visit to the country by a Canadian prime minister.

Carney will sit down with Turkish president Recep Tayyip Erdogan in Ankara Thursday, before heading to Istanbul for a series of business meetings. His office is not releasing who else he plans to meet with ahead of the trip.

While Reuters reports Canada and Türkiye will sign a joint declaration aimed at deepening ties in four areas including defence and energy, senior officials repeatedly declined to say what announcements are expected, beyond that something would be announced.

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

Another government source suggested what’s in the works is not finalized enough to the point of being able to share.

Officials did say the areas of trade focus include defence, energy, mining, tech and agriculture.

University of Ottawa international affairs Prof. Thomas Juneau calls Türkiye a “competitive autocracy” – too far removed to be considered a democracy.

The former Middle East policy analyst for the Department of National Defence agrees with the Carney government calculus that diversifying trade away from the United States requires going beyond dealing with pure democracies.

“The challenge, if, on moral grounds, we decide to limit our diversification efforts to democracies, is that there’s just not that many of them,” Juneau said.

“If we are to be serious in really being successful in diversifying our partnerships, trade and security, we simply must go beyond the small number of democracies, and that includes countries like Saudi Arabia, like Türkiye, with whom we do have common interests, but with whom we also do have serious disagreements,” Juneau told CTV News.

“Canada certainly engages with countries where we do not share 100 per cent of the values in all ways,” said one senior official at the briefing.

In July, speaking in Saudi Arabia on the same trip that saw him visit Ankara for this year’s NATO summit, Carney said he believes “lecturing countries from afar is an ineffective strategy.”

At the summit, Canada and Türkiye announced they were formally launching talks towards a free trade agreement.

Deepening ties with Türkiye has faced criticism, especially from Canada’s large Armenian diaspora.

“As Canadians, we’re very supportive of the government’s efforts to diversify trade relations. We just do not believe at all that Türkiye is the right partner,” Sevag Belian of the Armenian National Committee of Canada told CTV News, specifically mentioning human rights concerns and the country’s “destabilizing role” in the region.

Belian says the community is reacting to the trip with “alarm and concern.”

He says the biggest worry is that as part of the deepening of ties, Canada may reverse its stance on recognition of the Armenian genocide. Canada officially recognized the Armenian Genocide in 2004.

“We are very fearful that the Turkish side will put this issue on the table. But we are hopeful that the Canadian side won’t budge,” Belian says.

The University of Waterloo’s Bessma Momani doesn’t think the issue will be reopened.

But she tells CTV News, for the cost benefit analysis of dealing with Türkiye to be worth it, the trip must amount to more than a series of photo-ops.

“The way to make this worth it is to actually sign some real deals, investment, have corporations, both Canadian corporations investing in Türkiye, and similarly Turkish companies investing here-that will be the proof of success,” Momani said.

This summer, the government ran consultations allowing Canadians to weigh in on a potential free trade deal with Türkiye. While the processed wrapped up Sept. 14, a summary of what they found has not yet been released, and officials at the briefing declined to share a sense of the findings.

The defence relationship has been rocky, with Canada suspending arms export permits in 2020. A government report found evidence the country was using Canadian military technology, specifically sensors used on Turkish drones, in the conflict in the Nagorno-Karabakh region of Azerbaijan.

That ban was lifted in 2024, with Canada now assessing exports on a case-by-case basis.

“We are in a position to resume a more regular export relationship, and we will continue to monitor,” a government official said.

Carney will be joined on the trip by Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand and Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson. Anand visited Türkiye in March, and hosted her counterpart in Canada in June.

Canada has faced criticism for not specifically condemning the ongoing crackdown in Türkiye on LGBTQ2S+ groups. Anand has said that shouldn’t be interpreted as a lack of solidarity with oppressed people.

Tuesday, senior government officials pointed to Canada signing on to this Equal Rights Coalition statement condemning the persecution of LGBTIQ+ activists globally as a violation of human rights. It doesn’t specifically mention Türkiye.

Hodgson’s presence underlines the significance of Canada’s energy sector to the burgeoning trade relationship, though government officials would not say whether any deal to purchase Canadian CANDU reactor or SMRs was in the cards for this trip.

Türkiye is “desperate for energy,” says Momani, pointing to its reliance on “not trustworthy” countries like Iran and Russia in the past.

“They would very much like to have Western, NATO members to procure as much energy as possible, whether it’s nuclear or LNG or any other clean tech, all of it is something that I think Türkiye is desperately in need of,” she said.

Correction

A previous version of this story suggested Prime Minister Mark Carney’s last visit to Turkiye was at the G20 summit. In fact, his last visit came during the NATO summit last July.

items.title: Loss of BioWare, ‘legendary’ video game studio, hits like a gut punch: Digital Alberta
items.description: It’s the end of an age for Alberta’s only AAA video game studio as BioWare announced Wednesday it would be shutting down.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Cover art for the 'Mass Effect: Legendary Edition' game. (BioWare/Electronic Arts)]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: It’s the end of an age for Alberta’s only AAA video game studio as BioWare announced Wednesday it would be shutting down.
items.body:
The Reapers have come, spelling the end of an age for Alberta’s only AAA video game studio as BioWare announced Wednesday it would be shutting down.

The studio behind beloved games and franchises like Baldur’s Gate, Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, Mass Effect, and Dragon Age was founded in Edmonton in 1995.

“After more than three decades of shared adventures, BioWare is closing and early development on the next Mass Effect project is ending,” the studio wrote in an announcement online.

BioWare once also had offices across North America, including in Montreal, San Francisco, California, and Austin, Texas.

The company was acquired by Electronic Arts (EA) in 2007. Recently, EA was acquired by a group of buyers, including Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund and Affinity Partners, which is led by U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, according to the BBC.

The decision to shutter BioWare is being seen as a “cost-saving” measure and described as a “tremendous loss” by Travis Gibson, a vice chair with Digital Alberta.

“Today sucks. BioWare going down sucks. I can’t under use this word enough; it is a legendary studio,” Gibson said. “The initial feelings are obviously going to be raw. It’s a gut punch. I can’t imagine what the people on the floor of BioWare are feeling and going through right now.”

Edmonton Mayor Andrew Knack, who says Mass Effect is one of his all-time favourite game series, expressed sadness for the loss of the studio, laying the blame squarely on corporations.

“This has nothing to do with Edmonton; this has to do with their corporate company making that decision,” Knack added.

“We’ve been seeing Xbox laying off thousands of people over the last six months here. This industry has evolved significantly, and so it’s a shame to see how the video game industry has been impacted like this.”

How it started, how it ended

At one point, there were hundreds of people employed at BioWare, but the company got its start in the early ’90s with only six people.

“It was a bunch of clueless farm kids and city kids from Alberta deciding that, in an era where everybody thinks video games can only be made in California or Japan, maybe we can do it, too,” said BioWare co-founder and current CEO of Beamdog Trent Oster.

“We started work on a game called Shattered Steel … it did things in 1996 which people just hadn’t even heard of before,” he added.

“It was successful enough that we managed to greenlight our second title, which was Baldur’s Gate, and it was a resounding success, even though everybody told us it would not be.”

Oster left BioWare in 2009, two years after it was acquired by EA.

“EA wasn’t a good fit. There were just some fundamental misalignments,” Oster said.

“EA, at its core, is a monetization company. It takes franchises, it figures out how to extract money out of them on a regular basis for shareholder return. BioWare was an innovation company, long investment cycles, uncertain payoffs.”

Oster believes there were around 40 employees left at BioWare at the end, mainly those working on the now-cancelled fifth installment in the Mass Effect franchise.

“Having (BioWare) shut down, it’s a seismic blow to the local industry,” Oster said.

“You’ve got a lot of people who are really talented, who could have been in big mentoring roles throughout the local industry, and now many of them will probably have to move elsewhere for jobs because the Edmonton scene is quite small.”

Celebrating BioWare’s legacy

While upset about the closure, Knack wanted to emphasize the impact BioWare has had on Edmonton and the gaming industry over its 31 years.

“The video game industry is what it is today because of BioWare, and you can never replace them,” he said.

“Making games back in the ’90s when they started was incredibly hard and incredibly time-consuming, and they did something special pretty much with every single one of their games,” added Gibson.

“They made something almost purely for the gamer, and gamers really resonated with it, and they enjoyed it, and they loved it.”

As sad as many may be feeling over the loss of an industry-defining studio, Gibson hopes one day there may be a silver lining for gamers.

“Video games is still a very passionate industry, and we still have an incredible amount of talent in Alberta and in Edmonton specifically, and I’d hate for this talent to go and move industries if they don’t want to,” he said.

“Hopefully, in 10-, 20-years’ time, we have another equally, or if not better, legendary studio within Edmonton that we’re known for.”

Gibson added that Digital Alberta is ready to support those affected by the closure who may now be looking to find a new role in the industry, including opening their own studios.

Edmonton has a plethora of independent gaming studios with recent and upcoming releases, including studios with former BioWare employees like Studio Reset, Arcanaut Studios and Beamdog.

  • Achievement unlocked: Edmonton studios show off games in Germany

“This is essentially our mandate and our mission, and this is going to be our focus moving forward,” he added. “We get to grieve a little bit, we get to go and do another playthrough of Knights of the Old Republic, and then we get to move forward.”

With files from CTV News Edmonton’s Jeremy Thompson

items.title: Bill Clinton praises PM Carney, says Trump has treated Canada like ‘dirt’
items.description: Former U.S. president Bill Clinton considers Mark Carney a longtime friend and called the prime minister 'about the most well qualified leader in the world.'
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Left: Prime Minister Mark Carney (The Canadian Press). Centre: U.S. President Donald Trump. Right: Former U.S. president Bill Clinton (The Associated Press).]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: Former U.S. president Bill Clinton considers Mark Carney a longtime friend and called the prime minister 'about the most well qualified leader in the world.'
items.body:
Former U.S. president Bill Clinton considers Mark Carney a longtime friend and called the prime minister “about the most well qualified leader in the world.”

Clinton made the remarks Tuesday evening during a campaign event in Florida for David Jolly, the Democratic nominee for governor.

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

“I’m tired of treating our allies like they’re dirt,” he said, a reference to recent rhetoric from U.S. President Donald Trump against Canada.

“The prime minster of Canada has been a friend of mine for a long time … He’s about the most well-qualified leader in the world. He’s been head of the (central) bank both in the U.K. and Canada,” said Clinton.

“And we have the gall to suggest that they should become the 51st state?”

Trump has mused about turning Canada into a U.S. state for more than a year and has suggested his administration could use economic force to do so. He repeated the comment as recently as last week, during a rally in Bullhead City, Ariz.

“They’ll be doing something just like Greenland,” he said, adding that it “just adds to our beautiful plate,” referring to the U.S. Last January, the American leader ignited anxiety across NATO by demanding control over the Arctic Island of 55,000.

His tone toward Canada and its prime minister – whom he sometimes calls a governor – has ebbed and flowed as the two countries maneuver a trade war that has resulted in tariffs on a wide range of goods and layoffs, as companies north of the border move operations south.

On Wednesday, Carney announced a $9-billion joint plan with the government of Ontario to help industries hit by the trade war. It includes a $5-billion fund for the steel industry, $2.5 billion for the automotive sector and $1 billion for the Ring of Fire mining development in northern Ontario.

Clinton did not provide details regarding how he and Carney became friends, only saying “we got to know each other having virtually nothing to do with politics.”

Clinton’s presidency lasted from 1993 to 2001. At the time, Carney was working at Goldman Sachs. He moved to become the deputy governor of Canada’s central bank in 2003.

items._ogDesc: Prime Minister Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford have unveiled a nearly $9 billion in supports for the province’s tariff-hit auto and steel sectors.
items.body:
Prime Minister Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford have unveiled nearly $9 billion in supports for the province’s tariff-hit auto and steel sectors.

The commitments under the “new action plan” include $5 billion to help upgrade Ontario steel mills and $2.5 billion to help the province’s ailing auto industry pivot to electric vehicle production.

There is also $1 billion to help build roads to the mineral-rich Ring of Fire region in Northern Ontario.

The prime minister framed the plan as part of ongoing efforts to bolster Canada’s economy in the face of a drawn-out trade war with the United States.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war has dragged on for more than a year-and-a-half, slamming key Canadian sectors, including automotive and steel manufacturing.

“U.S. tariffs have upended a trade bargain that’s existed for decades. They have raised costs for American families while putting Ontario workers and businesses at a disadvantage and under a cloud of uncertainty,” Carney said during a joint news conference with Ford in Ottawa on Wednesday afternoon.

“We can’t control what others do, so we are focusing on what we can control—and building Canada strong at home and diversifying our partnerships abroad.”

Carney said the investments would help to create 70,000 jobs linked to the Ring of Fire and protect some 220,000 linked to the other industries.

“Protecting what we have is not enough. We must go further. To transform our economy. To secure our future,” the prime minister said.

Premier Ford welcomed the “historic agreement,” which will see Ontario pitching in $2.67 billion.

“As we stand here today, it’s clear that Canada’s relationship with the United States has changed permanently,” Ford said.

“No matter what happens in the midterms, no matter who sits in the White House, we’re not going back to the way things were, and we need to plan accordingly.”

What’s in the action plan?

The two levels of government are launching the Joint Steel Action Fund, which they said will support the steel industry to make products that many Canadian companies need.

“We have the best steelworkers in the world and vast natural resources. Yet we import over 6.5 million tonnes of steel a year. Often that’s because we don’t make the steel Canadian companies need. It’s time to be our own best customer,” Carney said.

The federal government is also strengthening CBSA enforcement to protect against foreign steel dumping.

“When Canadian projects need specialized steel, they can increasingly count on Canadian mills and Canadian steelworkers to supply it,” the prime minister said.

The federal government also announced that it would freeze Canada’s fleet average performance standard at 172 grams per mile for new light-duty vehicles through 2029. Annual increases will resume in the 2030 model year line.

The freeze, the government said, would provide manufacturers with “near-term flexibility at a time when the industry is facing trade-related pressures.”

“Ontario and Canada are being challenged right now. We see it in every corner of our province, where tariffs and trade uncertainty are leaving workers and their families worried. But my message is very simple: working together, we will be there to support you no matter what,” Ford said.

“Today’s agreement will fortify and transform these sectors to become the foundation of our future prosperity.”

With files from The Canadian Press

Correction

A previous version of this story suggested that the $8.7 billion in funding was coming solely from the federal government. The aid package is made up of funding from both the Ontario and federal governments.

items.description: For thousands of years, Indigenous peoples have passed down their traditions and culture through oral storytelling. Now, a Canadian Indigenous community is using a data centre to help preserve its heritage.

items._ogDesc: For thousands of years, Indigenous peoples have passed down their traditions and culture through oral storytelling. Now, a Canadian Indigenous community is using a data centre to help preserve its heritage.
items.body:
For thousands of years, Indigenous peoples have passed down their traditions and culture through oral storytelling. Now, a Canadian Indigenous community is using a data centre to help preserve its heritage.

The Wiikwemkoong Unceded Territory in rural Ontario installed a small data centre as it modernized its recordkeeping systems. Among the digital files it holds are video recordings of Anishinaabe speaking their native language.

“Our language is one of the biggest things that most First Nations across the country are losing,” said Wiikwemkoong Chief Tim Ominika. “We will have our knowledge keepers, our language speakers who may be moving on to the spirit world, but their legacy is still going to be protected for many years to come by having our own data systems in place and protecting that.”

The idea of digital sovereignty has gained momentum in places like Europe, where leaders are wary of the widespread influence of American Big Tech. For the Wiikwemkoong and other Indigenous communities, it is also about asserting authority over their own information after historically being excluded from its collection and use by colonizers.

About the size of a single-car garage, the data centre installed last year also stores the community’s corporate documents, health data for residents, and security camera footage.

“The purpose of all of this is having the ownership, access, control and possession of our information,” Ominika said. It’s about preventing anyone else from “having authority or setting their guidelines on what they could do with our data.”

The Indigenous community has been transferring all its information from a Microsoft data centre in Toronto, 305 kilometres south, said Michael McCormick, the community’s chief technical officer.

Other Indigenous communities have been taking an interest

Wiikwemkoong is on the eastern end of Manitoulin Island in Lake Huron, an area that attracts visitors with its rugged wilderness, extensive waterways and Anishinaabe cultural offerings. The reserve prides itself on being Canada’s only “unceded territory,” because it never signed a treaty surrendering its land.

The data centre, which underpins a modernization of Wiikwemkoong’s administrative services, also has paved the way for new public safety infrastructure, including a drone fleet and a network of surveillance cameras. A backup data centre on the mainland and public Wi-Fi transmitters are also planned for the community of about 4,000 people. The chief declined to disclose how much is being spent on the projects.

Improvements to data storage gained urgency after a flood in 2022 resulted in the loss of some of its digital records, which had been scattered in various offices.

“That information is very important to us. And in order to protect it, keep it safe, we said ’Why can’t we not look at developing and creating and implementing our own data sovereignty program?’” Ominika said.

Wiikwemkoong’s upgrade program is among the first for Indigenous communities in Canada that include First Nations, Inuit and Métis. Delegations from other Indigenous communities in Ontario and neighboring Manitoba have come to check out the project, McCormick said.

The chief said he has to explain to visitors that their data centre is not like the giant ones relied on by artificial intelligence companies that require vast amounts of land and water.

Wiikwemkoong’s data centre sits in a secure bunker next to the administrative office, accessed by a facial recognition scanner. Its four racks of computer servers are cooled by a pair of fans — not water — and it has “a relatively small carbon footprint,” McCormick said.

In the U.S., a few Native American tribes like the Navajo Nation have for years been operating their own data centres for local infrastructure services.

Wiikwemkoong’s data centre is believed to be the only one on Indigenous territory in Canada, but McCormick said other Indigenous leaders are increasingly savvy about control of their data. The Chiefs of Ontario, which represents 133 First Nations in the province, held a data sovereignty conference earlier this year that included a panel on AI and data centres.

For generations, Indigenous communities worldwide have had no say in how information on them has been collected, interpreted and held by governments, researchers and institutions, said Carmen Jones, director of research and data management for the Chiefs of Ontario.

“As more information is collected and stored, it is critical that First Nations determine how that data is accessed, managed, and used,” she said.

The technology has addressed some issues — and raised new ones

Amid the island’s natural splendor, the community faces its share of problems that community leaders hope the technology can help address.

Since installing the data centre, McCormick’s team has added 700 surveillance cameras around the community, and a dozen drone docking stations on the administrative office’s rooftop housing a fleet of DJI drones. They are used to find people who go missing in the area’s wooded hills, look out for criminal activity, such as drug deals and break-ins, and monitor for forest fires.

Ominika said there was “a little bit of resistance” to the drone program from residents worried about privacy.

Wiikwemkoong’s drones are supplied by DJI, a Chinese company whose drones have been blocked in the United States over national security concerns. McCormick said all drone footage would be stored locally. The chief said he wanted to make sure any information the drones collect “is going to be protected” and not ”used against us, moving forward, by China.”

First Nations in Canada recognized the importance of data sovereignty decades ago, drawing up their own data governance principles in 1998 because they were often the focus of research by outsiders that didn’t benefit them. That argument is reflected in current criticism of Big Tech companies building AI large language models by scraping text, video, images and other data from the internet, often without permission.

Ominika said community leaders would be cautious and thoughtful when considering the use of AI.

“Once we start to realize and understand that there is a potential of any kind of resistance or harm towards our community, then we would put a stop there,” he said.

Kelvin Chan, The Associated Press

Cara McKenna of IndigiNews contributed to this report.

items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Atlas Engineered Products unveils Canada’s first robotic roof truss manufacturing line, located in Vanastra, Ont. on Oct. 21, 2026. (Scott Miller/CTV News London)]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: The announcement was made Wednesday by Sarnia-Lambton MP Marilyn Gladu on behalf of Energy and Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson during a groundbreaking ceremony at the site.
items.body:
You’re looking at Canada’s first robotic roof truss manufacturing line, and it is located in Huron County, Ont.

“The robotics go slower than human beings, but they’re consistent,” said the Founder and President of Atlas Engineered Products, Hadi Abassi.

Abassi bought Clinton Truss in 2018, with the idea of revolutionizing how roof trusses were built in Canada. Two years ago, he started construction of this $20 million facility in Vanastra, Ont., to robotically manufacture roof trusses, streamlining the production process from start to finish.

“And not just trusses. We have the same system, and same vision for the component construction, for the walls section and floor sections,” said Abassi.

With 10 factories across Canada, Abassi aims to build homes piece by piece, and deliver them to construction sites across North America, speeding up the on-site home construction process.

“We will take a set of plans. We will break it out. We build it like a jigsaw puzzle. Very simple puzzle. So instead of taking three or four months to build from the foundation up, we can do this with the installation crew in four to five days,” said Abassi.

For the previous founder and former owner of Clinton Truss, Harvey Poirier, seeing his former company on the cutting edge of truss construction is nothing short of astounding.

“We heard them talking about this about two years ago or something like it. It looks pretty good so far,” said Poirier.

Huron East Mayor Bernie MacLellan says he’s happy to see a company started 28 years ago moving into the future and doing so in Huron County.

“People didn’t understand that it was in Vanastra, but they had a great reputation to begin with. And now they’re just taking it to the next level and doing automation that nobody else in Canada has ever done before,” said MacLellan.

Abassi says they’ll have a mix of manual and robotic truss manufacturing for the time being, with an expansion of jobs from the current 40 employees in the near future.

“We’re hoping that we can double that very soon. Right now, we have asked for 20 more people for this facility. You cannot do it without human beings, but it’s a great compliment to the human being. You still need the race car drivers, but you have an amazing car to drive now,” said Abassi.

Helping to enable the expansion in Vanastra, a $4 million grant from Natural Resources Canada’s Forestry Innovation Support Program.

items.description:
Canadian real estate remains out of reach for young adults, but the show must go on. That’s the takeaway from a new housing report from National Bank of Canada. Slow home sales have led to a backlog of developer inventory, but billions in public bailouts are being used to support prices. National Bank urges policymakers […]

The post Canadian Real Estate Needs More Immigration, Foreign Buyers: National Bank appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: National Bank warns Canada’s housing market needs higher immigration and foreign buyers to clear a record inventory of unsold homes and avoid a demographic cliff.
items.body:
Canadian real estate remains out of reach for young adults, but the show must go on. That’s the takeaway from a new housing report from National Bank of Canada. Slow home sales have led to a backlog of developer inventory, but billions in public bailouts are being used to support prices. National Bank urges policymakers to increase their immigration targets and reintroduce foreign buyers to help developers reduce inventory.

Canadian Real Estate In A Slump Despite Billions In Bailouts

The Great Canadian Real Estate Slump isn’t exactly news, but not everyone may be aware of how slow it’s been. Over 1 in 4 (28%) newly completed homes remain unsold, charting new territory for excess supply. “The inventory of completed and unsold housing units across all census metropolitan areas stands at 20,700 units, its highest level since records began in 1990,” warns the bank.

Existing homes aren’t doing much better. Seasonally adjusted sales saw a monthly drop of 2.3% in September, sliding 13% below the 10-year average. While Canadian home prices are now in the biggest correction on record, the almost 5-year slump only rolled back 13 months of price gains. That’s with taxpayer-backed bailouts.

“This demonstrates that the market is so weak that it requires public support,” writes National Bank.

Policymakers aren’t dabbling in support either—they’re fully immersed in the practice. The bank cites Ontario’s $1.3 billion bailout to help investors buy 2,200 unsold Toronto condos. They also cite Ottawa and British Columbia’s $1.45 billion program for roughly the same number of condos. These programs are massive, but even taxpayer-funded bulk buying isn’t enough to clear the backlog.

The bank urges policymakers to drum up more demand. Not from the young adults struggling with shelter costs. They can’t afford to buy a home. They’re calling on Ottawa to look beyond its borders to support prices. Seriously.

Big Six Bank Calls For Higher Immigration To Improve Demand

Canadian real estate prices surged from 2020 and finally peaked in March 2022. That occurred during the pandemic’s population slump, when population growth plummeted to near historic lows. Canada ramped up immigration to unprecedented levels as the slump kicked off. Despite a timing mismatch, reduced immigration is often cited as extending the downturn. The narrative was reinforced by StatCan’s population estimates that revealed a historic contraction. However, that contraction also didn’t happen.

The agency’s recent revisions show the 0.5% y/y decline reported at the start of 2026 was actually 0.5% growth. Ottawa’s plan to reduce non-permanent residents (NPR) to 5% of the population by 2027 is also unlikely. Not only did policymakers delay the target by a year, but NPRs currently represent 6.7% of the population. Canada needs to lose roughly 750,000 NPRs by the end of next year to make those numbers work. Still, the Big Six Bank is concerned.

Reducing NPRs to 5% of the total population will slow total growth to 0.2% in 2027 and 0.1% in 2028, notes the bank. They warn that sticking to the target will mean more downward pressure on housing. “In that context, we believe Ottawa should recalibrate its immigration policy through a targeted and gradual increase in immigration levels,” says National Bank.

Canadians Can’t Afford Homes? Sell Them To Foreign Investors

Canada’s foreign homebuyer restrictions are set to expire in a few months. “The ban on foreign home purchases, which expires on January 1, 2027, should not be extended but rather replaced by a more flexible policy,” explains National Bank.

Whether Canada will renew the moratorium is unclear, but policymakers aren’t fond of the measures. They began to quietly ease foreign buyer restrictions just 86 days after boasting of passing the ban. Canada has since elected Prime Minister Mark Carney, and while he hasn’t addressed the ban directly, the bank notes he recently laid the groundwork for a “controlled increase” in the population.

One of his key fundraisers in BC has been a little more vocal about foreign capital returning to housing. Shortly after PM Carney was elected, Vancouver’s “condo king” said he was working with the PM to drum up foreign capital for rentals.

National Bank sees foreign buyers as one of the only ways developers can sell the homes they built. “We believe it should not be renewed in its current form and that a more flexible model—such as Australia’s, which notably allows foreign buyers to purchase new homes—would help reduce the inventory of unsold housing,” argues the bank.

The bank’s take seems tone-deaf, but the implications are more disturbing. RBC recently found the average first-time buyer plans to buy at 41, 12 years later than current owners did. Separately, they found parents are increasingly helping their adult kids pay bills—a trend most parents attribute to a soaring cost of living rather than poor money management.

Canada’s young adults have been locked out of the housing market. For years they were told that more supply would close the gap, and building more would finally bring prices down. After taxpayers footed the bill to accelerate construction, the narrative abruptly shifted: prices can’t fall further because developers can’t make the math work. Since young adults can’t afford these prices, we suddenly need more temporary residents to support attractive rents that developers can pitch to foreign landlords.

items.description: Desjardins sees Ontario buyers returning, but a Bank of Canada hike could cut the recovery short
items.content: <p>Desjardins sees Ontario buyers returning, but a Bank of Canada hike could cut the recovery short</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639282053551425211.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Desjardins sees Ontario buyers returning, but a Bank of Canada hike could cut the recovery short
items.body:
Ontario’s housing market is set for a modest recovery in 2027, with Desjardins Group forecasting a near-5% rise in existing home sales. However, a looming Bank of Canada rate increase could erode the affordability gains brokers are only starting to see.

In its Ontario Housing Outlook, Desjardins senior economist Kari Norman projects provincial resales will reach about 167,000 units next year, up 4.7%, while the average price edges up 2.4% to roughly $825,000.

Lower prices, rising incomes, first-time buyer supports and pent-up demand should pull buyers back, though activity will stay well below long-term norms.

What a Bank of Canada hike would mean for Ontario borrowers

Desjardins expects two quarter-point increases, starting in late October. The central bank has held its overnight rate at 2.25% since October 2025, and its next decision lands October 28 as markets price in a growing likelihood of Bank of Canada rate hikes.

Grant Armstrong, chief growth officer at WealthOne Bank of Canada, saw the same signals at MortgageFest 2026.

“I think rates will probably go up in October. GIC rates are up 35 points in the last sixty to ninety days. Bank of Canada bond rates are up 60 points,” he said.

Stéfane Marion, chief economist at National Bank of Canada in Montréal, is less convinced. “I don’t think that the Bank of Canada should be hiking next week, and if they do hike, they can’t be too aggressive,” he told the Mortgage Professionals Canada conference in Calgary, where he also urged brokers to steer clients toward the five-year fixed mortgage.

Daren King of National Bank of Canada and Penelope Graham of Ratehub .ca say five-year fixed-rate mortgages have fallen to a record-low share of new lending as more borrowers opt for variable-rate and shorter-term products. https://t.co/CVKUTrrUL5 — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 13, 2026

First-time buyers step into the gap

Toronto’s condo slump remains the biggest drag. Only 525 condo units were started in the City of Toronto in the first nine months of 2026, against nearly 14,000 a year over the previous decade, the report said – a collapse that has left many presale condo buyers facing appraisal shortfalls and lost deposits.

Temporary HST relief of up to $130,000 and Toronto development-charge cuts of 40% to 60% through August 2029 aim to restart activity.

For end users, the reset is an opening. “For people who actually need to buy real estate for their own use, I think that’s really the best time to get into the market,” Christine Xu, founder of Money Broker Canada, said at MortgageFest.

Sarita Free, a mortgage agent with Mortgage Powered Financial Group in Norfolk County, Ontario, sees the same shift.

“With the 30-year amortization that we can now go to, I find a lot of my buyers that have been on the sidelines are finally able to break into the market and stay in their hometown,” she said.

Desjardins projects housing starts will rise about 6% to nearly 65,000 units in 2027, still more than 30% below 2021 and 2022 levels. Norman flagged Canada-US trade tensions and Middle East-driven oil prices as key risks.

items.title: Province pays private developers a premium to acquire key sites
items.description: Specific requirements often push governments to overvalue real estate
items._ogDesc: Specific requirements often push governments to overvalue real estate
items.body:
How much should governments pay to acquire land?

Under the BC NDP, the province has acquired several private properties for public use, paying what some industry sources describe as an unusual premium.

In fall 2025, the province announced that it had allocated $26 million to the Conseil scolaire francophone de la Colombie-Britannique to acquire 3044 Pratt St., Abbotsford, for a Francophone school. Provincial transaction data records a purchase price from a subsidiary of Abbotsford’s Azure Properties Group of $24.6 million, or $2 million an acre (leaving $1.4 million to cover transaction and closing costs).

On Jan. 29, the province acquired a 40-acre property at 1320 McKenzie Rd., Abbotsford, from a subsidiary of Richmond’s Panatch Group for $27.8 million, or $695,000 an acre. The property was used to grow vegetables, but Infrastructure BC plans to build a new Plant and Animal Health Centre on the site in partnership with the B.C. Ministry of Agriculture and Food.

On March 31, Crown corporation BC Hydro acquired a 21.75-acre parcel of vacant industrial land at 2161 Caribou Drive, Langford, from Vancouver-based developers Strand and Bastion Development Corp. for $52.5 million, or an average of $2.4 million an acre.

Howard Chai, who broke news of the deal at The Realist, noted that the “very specific” real estate needs of public entities often result in them appearing to pay more for sites than what other, less constrained parties might.

In the case of the school site in Abbotsford, industry sources indicate that the price was well above not just the $9.8 million value the BC Assessment assigned it on July 1, 2025, but also previous offers by private developers.

One well-known Vancouver developer who spoke to Western Investor on condition of anonymity, considered acquiring the property after it returned to market in fall 2022. Plans filed with the city at the time called for 130 townhomes on a developable area of seven acres. Pricing guidance stood at $24 million.

However, the site’s challenging topography, marked by steep slopes and fish-bearing streams, left just 3.5 acres suitable for development in the view of the developer. It couldn’t justify a price greater than $10 million.

An accepted offer in the range of $18 million ultimately came through, but during the due diligence process the purchaser reduced the offer to $15.5 million—again, because of site considerations. The deal collapsed.

An industry source familiar with the details—also speaking anonymously—called the price the province paid “crazy” and “a ridiculous amount of money,” especially for a property that would need to be rezoned before a school could be built.

“It’s a massive risk,” the source said, noting that Abbotsford has historically been reluctant to tweak its Official Community Plan to accommodate new uses within established zones.

Similarly, the province paid several times Farm Credit Canada’s reported regional average of $104,600 for agricultural parcels last year to acquire the farmland for the new Plant and Animal Health Centre. With farmland values in B.C. declining over the past 18 months, the province’s premium looks even more egregious.

While the purchase price was “well below” the prices of nearby retail or industrial properties, the site was purchased as actively farmed land within the Agricultural Land Reserve that would require a non-farm use application.

“Why the province paid so dearly for it, relative to what Panatch paid in 2020, is a bit of a mystery,” said Paul Richter, director of market analytics with CoStar. “They did go through the process to get ALC approval to subdivide into two parcels, and for ‘non-farm use’ approvals to permit the [Plant and Animal Health] Centre. This could have added value, for the right buyer. In this case, the only buyer that would have likely stepped up, stepped up. The province.”

The spending practices of other levels of government offer a point of comparison for the province’s land acquisitions.

The Department of National Defence acquired two multi-family properties on Vancouver Island last year to house personnel. A newly built 37-unit property at 244 Island Highway in View Royal traded in early October 2025 for $23.4 million, or an average of $631,622 per door unit—the most expensive multi-family transaction in Greater Victoria last year, according to CBRE Ltd. statistics.

Near CFB Comox, DND bought a 52-unit property at 574 Cumberland Rd., Courtenay, from Simba Investments Ltd. for $19.1 million. The purchase price averaged $367,308 a door—a premium versus the Mid-Island average at mid-year as reported by CBRE of $200,938 per door.

Within the Lower Mainland, the City of Coquitlam paid $3 million—or an average of $16.7 million per acre—in August 2025 for a 0.18-acre medium-density residential development site at 570 Austin Ave., Coquitlam.

The various government transactions, all completed within a few months of one another and involving different asset types, show a willingness to spend well beyond what the private sector would pay.

“It’s definitely a trend,” said the industry source familiar with the history of the Pratt Road site. “With half the developers I have done business with over the years, it’s well known that if they’re moving forward with a property, it’s because they’ve done their due diligence and they know that they can make money doing this. And they do that because they’re responsible for their own private capital and don’t want to lose money.”

items.title: Global mobility’s compliance blind spots are costing organizations
items.description: As cross-border work normalizes, employers face a mounting immigration, tax, and reputational exposure without adequate governance in place
items.content: <p>As cross-border work normalizes, employers face a mounting immigration, tax, and reputational exposure without adequate governance in place</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/036/0287_639281217985765444.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: As cross-border work normalizes, employers face a mounting immigration, tax, and reputational exposure without adequate governance in place
items.body:
The way Canadian organizations manage their people’s movement across borders has changed fundamentally – and most HR teams haven’t kept pace. As cross-border work shifts from structured international assignments to informal arrangements involving remote work, frequent business travel, and digital nomad arrangements, compliance obligations have multiplied without a corresponding evolution in governance.

The risks are unlike anything the industry has previously navigated, says Jack Kim, Partner in the Toronto office of Fragomen, a global immigration services firm. “The global mobility environment is quite in flux and you have a lot of tensions grappling against each other,” says Kim. He says that demand for global talent is surging in priority sectors including defence, energy, and infrastructure, but political headwinds at home and abroad are complicating access to that talent as enforcement tightens worldwide.

The data underscores the problem. According to global workforce management firm ECA’s Global Mobility Now 2026 study, two-thirds of global employers have no formal process for reviewing compliance implications, such as immigration limits or internal company thresholds. With nearly half of organizations in the study expecting business travel to increase and international remote work to grow over the next two years, that gap is only widening.

When informal mobility becomes a liability

Compliance problems rarely begin with a policy failure, says Kim. More often, they start with a routine trip. An employee travels repeatedly to a client in the U.S. A specialist is dispatched to an overseas facility under no formal assignment structure. None of these situations looks like a traditional global mobility file – but each can trigger payroll obligations, immigration requirements and corporate tax exposure simultaneously, he says.

“Especially on the tax front, it’s a pain in the butt to track where are my employees on any given day,” Kim says, noting that technology helps but there are also cultural questions to be considered. “And that has increased the need for employers to be able to do exactly what governments are trying to do. Where is a person on any given day? Are there a certain number of days that trigger a tax complication or an immigration complication as well? And then how do I do it?”

When individual non-compliance goes undetected, the consequences rarely stay contained. Kim points to a recent U.S. enforcement action at a battery plant in Atlanta involving a Korean company, as a cautionary example of how quickly a workforce issue becomes a geopolitical one. “Hundreds of people were apprehended at the same time, and it caused lots of news stories and consternation from governments,” he says. “It turned into a bilateral issue and a geopolitical issue.”

Kim cautions Canadian organizations against treating such scenarios as distinctly American. “This could also happen in different countries as well because the number one question, especially in countries that are facing populist-type movements, is that they don’t want people to be working illegally inside their country, and no political party wants to own that as part of a scandal.”

The case for centralized mobility governance

The decentralized approach many organizations default to – leaving individual entities or regional HR teams to manage their own immigration processes independently – is no longer adequate. Leaving immigration or compliance processes siloed across business units or provinces is a structural liability at this stage of regulatory complexity, according to Kim. “Those days are probably over because of all the complexities that you have to think about, and the dependencies between everything that happens,” he says.

Greater visibility at the executive level is equally important. Kim uses the example of a travel ban enacted by Canada during a public health emergency in Africa from Ebola to illustrate how a mobility gap becomes a leadership crisis overnight. “If you don’t know where your people are, and if you have a facility in the Democratic Republic of Congo, then you need to know who’s there right now visiting, and that immediately becomes a C-suite issue, whether you like it or not.”

The model Kim advocates is cross-functional by design, integrating immigration, tax, travel management, technology and HR business partners into a unified framework. Organizations building cross-border workforce compliance frameworks that address immigration, tax, and travel risk, as well as balance global hiring with cross-border compliance obligations, are better placed to manage the dependencies that determine whether international moves succeed or stall, he says.

“Those things should be thought of at the front end of decision-making, not at the back end,” Kim says. “Be proactive about these things, increasing visibility within your own companies, having policies in place and game planning, crisis control – because more often than not, as we've seen with the wars going on in the Middle East and in Ukraine, there's some more strategic planning that needs to be done and you cannot be reactive anymore.”

Canada’s regulatory reset and what it means for HR

Canada’s immigration system is itself in transition. Tighter temporary resident targets and the pending transfer of International Mobility Program (IMP) compliance oversight from Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) to Employment and Social Development Canada (ESDC) signal a more enforcement-focused posture from Ottawa for employers navigating the process of hiring foreign workers.

Kim describes the recalibration that began in 2024 as “in spirit necessary” – a response to documented system fraud, housing shortages, and strained school capacity. But he warns that the recalibration must be carefully managed. “What we need to do as a country going forward is to think of things in a much more intentional and calculated manner, strategic,” he says.

He points to a recent government initiative prioritizing permanent residence pathways for high-wage workers as a constructive signal, but stresses that Canada’s capacity needs make continued access to international talent non-negotiable. “We want to build submarines, but we’re contracting a foreign company to build them for us for the next 30 years,” he says. “If we want to build pipelines, then we need people to help us build those because the talent doesn’t all reside in Canada.”

With below-replacement birth rates now recorded across 37 of 38 Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) countries according to the OECD’s Pensions at a Glance 2025 report, the competition for skilled talent will only intensify. HR leaders monitoring Canada’s evolving immigration policy landscape and its impact on workforce strategy should treat government engagement – through their own C-suite or government relations functions – as a core part of their long-term planning, according to Kim.

“We’re going to be competing for the same people across the world for years to come,” he says.

Duty of care in a volatile world

As geopolitical risk becomes a standard feature of the global operating environment, duty of care for internationally mobile employees has shifted from a compliance consideration to a strategic imperative. Kim, who was involved in emergency evacuation efforts during the Taliban’s seizure of Kabul in 2021, knows precisely what inadequate planning looks like. “That was a real frantic couple of weeks when we were trying to get people out of the country,” he says.

Knowing where employees are, what travel authorizations they hold, and where they can be safely relocated is foundational. Organizations can plan for global immigration and labour mobility trends in advance – mapping visa-free travel options, identifying jurisdictions where an entity can provide temporary shelter and defining what a safe relocation pathway looks like before a crisis demands one. HR teams developing proactive duty-of-care and crisis response programs for internationally mobile employees are increasingly setting the standard expected by both regulators and the workforce itself.

As enforcement intensifies globally – such as stricter border rules that could impact business travellers – Kim says the penalties for non-compliance will follow. “Companies are more in the crosshairs too,” he says, pointing to major corporations in the U.S. that have faced restrictions on sponsoring foreign workers following fraud-related allegations. The reputational damage, he notes, arrives well before any verdict.

“Whether those allegations have been proven or not is a different thing, but once you’re in the headlines, you’re in the headlines,” says Kim. “And so these things will likely be used more at a higher level to cut things off at the pass.”

items.title: Ottawa is selling homes fast – but building the wrong kind
items.description: A record sales run is raising questions about what gets built next in Ottawa
items.content: <p>A record sales run is raising questions about what gets built next in Ottawa</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639281937065157840.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: A record sales run is raising questions about what gets built next in Ottawa
items.body:
Ottawa’s new home market posted its strongest September in recent memory, with 521 sales recorded. That's an 81.5% increase from the 287 transactions closed in September 2025, according to data from the Greater Ottawa Home Builders’ Association (GOHBA) and PMA Brethour Realty Group.

Month-over-month, activity climbed 12.3% from August’s 464 units. Year-to-date, 4,078 new homes have sold in Ottawa through September, up 53.8% from 2,652 at the same point last year.

Supply gap persists despite record sales pace

Housing starts in Ottawa are up 14% in 2026, with 8,169 homes under construction compared with 7,168 in the same period last year, according to the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC).

However, the gains have not kept pace with demand for ownership housing. Much of that pipeline is weighted toward rental, raising the prospect that Ottawa’s affordability recovery could go into reverse if the ownership supply gap continues to widen.

Jason Burggraaf, Executive Director of the Greater Ottawa Home Builders’ Association in Ontario, said September’s gains carry an important caveat.

“September’s sales are encouraging, but CMHC’s latest report shows Ottawa still faces a widening housing supply gap, with much of its construction activity concentrated in rentals,” Burggraaf said.

“Improving affordability means supporting more ownership housing too. Finalizing the development charge reduction agreement is an immediate opportunity to lower building costs, and we’re pushing for a timely resolution so some 2026 construction can benefit.”

The concern echoes comments Burggraaf made on Ottawa’s August new home sales results, when he cautioned, “Governments need to ensure that the way we fund growth doesn’t add costs that put those homes further out of reach.”

Geographically, Ottawa’s west end captured 43% of September sales, with the south at 40%, together accounting for 83% of all transactions.

The east recorded 15% and Central Ottawa 2%. Townhomes led all product types at 44%, followed by single-detached homes at 35% and condo townhomes at 20%.

Development charge relief within reach

City council approved a plan in July to reduce development charges by 54% over three years, tied to a joint federal-Ontario infrastructure fund.

Under that framework, charges on single-family and semi-detached homes inside the Greenbelt would fall to $25,752, with suburban builds set at $28,781.

Development charges are one-time fees levied on new residential properties to fund growth-related capital infrastructure.

The push to finalise the agreement comes as Canada’s housing affordability reached a four-year best in Q1 2026, according to RBC Economics, with the national aggregate measure falling to 53% of pre-tax median household income required to cover ownership costs.

items.title: Canadian consumer confidence climbs, but housing optimism lags
items.description: Home price optimism trails as brokers brace for the Bank of Canada’s October 28 decision
items.content: <p>Home price optimism trails as brokers brace for the Bank of Canada’s October 28 decision</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639281927714349803.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Home price optimism trails as brokers brace for the Bank of Canada’s October 28 decision
items.body:
Canadian consumer confidence firmed in mid-October, yet Canadians’ outlook for home values, the measure that matters most to mortgage brokers, still sits well below its historical norm.

The Bloomberg Nanos Canadian Confidence Index (BNCCI) reached 51.68 for the four weeks ending October 16, up from 49.86 a month earlier.

The weekly gauge is compiled from a rolling telephone survey of 1,016 Canadians. It sits above the neutral 50 mark but below its long-run average of 54.66 since 2008.

Almost all of the improvement came from the forward-looking side of the survey.

"The improvement was driven largely by brighter expectations: that sub-index climbed to 48.41 from 44.82. Pocketbook confidence, covering personal finances and job security, was broadly unchanged at 54.94," said Nik Nanos, chief data scientist at Nanos Research.

"Even so, overall confidence remains below its long-run average of 54.66, suggesting Canadians are feeling somewhat better, but remain cautious about the economic outlook as the year moves ahead."

What do Canadians expect from home prices?

The Expectations Index combines views on the economy with views on neighbourhood real estate, and the housing component remains soft.

Just 29.10% of respondents expect local home values to rise over the next six months. That is below the 2026 average of 34.28% and the long-run average of 39.76%.

Another 45.65% expect prices to hold, while 19.96% anticipate a decline.

Household finances offer little cushion. Only 11.03% said their personal finances improved over the past year, compared with 37.91% who said they were worse off.

British Columbia was the only region in net-negative territory, at 46.02. Ontario sat just under neutral at 49.91.

A new international research by Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) revealed that Canada’s inflation-adjusted home prices more than doubled between 2005 and 2025, rising 101% and outpacing every major peer country.

Fausto Gaudio of IC Savings argues that home prices remain too disconnected from incomes, making it increasingly difficult for first-time buyers to enter the market and highlighting the need for a broader affordability reset. https://t.co/3PehdHgrJn — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 13, 2026

How the confidence data fits the Bank of Canada rate call

Nanos said the Expectations Index has tracked year-over-year GDP growth with a 0.82 correlation on a six-month lag, and that the data has been cited in the Bank of Canada’s Monetary Policy Report. That makes the reading a timely input one week before the central bank’s October 28 decision. The overnight rate has stood at 2.25% since October 2025.

Most of the bank economists calling for an October 28 rate hold point to September’s inflation data.

Sherry Cooper, chief economist at Dominion Lending Centres Group, addressed those figures amid rising business inflation expectations in the Bank’s latest survey.

“The September data support our base-case scenario that the Bank of Canada will remain on hold at its October 28 meeting,” she said.

Stéfane Marion, chief economist at National Bank of Canada in Montréal, has urged brokers to recommend the five-year fixed over variable. He was direct about the risk of tightening. 

“I don’t think that the Bank of Canada should be hiking next week, and if they do hike, they can’t be too aggressive,” he noted.

items.title: Feeling Creative? Good Bones Hit The Trinity Bellwoods Market
items.description:
Our typical listing spotlight features the standard bells and whistles, including savvy staging. But sometimes, all it takes to make the eyes (and heart) linger is a bare-bones set of photos and a strong foundation.

This is the case with 13 Euclid Avenue. Tucked north of Queen, just around the corner from Trinity Bellwoods Park, this duplex — asking $999,700 — hits the market with its upper levels presenting as a clean state. With no staging, renderings, or AI imaginings (phew), the home can’t hide.

But with quality craftsmanship, that's not a problem.

Across 2.5 storeys, multiple elements feel (and may just be) straight from a past era. On arrival, you’re met by original hardwood flooring, which continues to make appearances across other areas of the home (including the top-floor bedroom — more on that shortly).

Original millwork, detailed plaster ceilings that soar to generous heights, and large windows that fill the space with natural light all bring a special type of character that’s difficult to emulate in a new build.

  • SPECS

    • Address: 13 Euclid Avenue, Toronto
    • Bedrooms: 4
    • Bathrooms: 2
    • Size: 1,500-2,000 sq. ft
    • Listed At: $999,700

The address is a working duplex; the lower unit — complete with its own kitchen and walkout to the backyard — is home to a tenant who, according to the listing, is happy to stay in place.

Make no mistake: there’s room for renovation and upgrades here, too. Whether it’s transforming the upper kitchen into an eat-in paradise, or combining landscaping with outdoor furniture to create a private backyard sanctuary, your imagination is the limit. But please, buyer-to-be — leave the blue bathroom tile intact.

______________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________

Our Favourite Thing

We've already given the bathroom tile its flowers, so here we'll celebrate the main top-level bedroom. Spanning some half of the home's top floor, this room features hardwood planks that are wider than elsewhere in the home — and we're swooning over them. Pair that floor with the uniquely angular ceiling, a skylight, and the quirky shelf built into the wall, and you have the perfect place to design a primary-bedroom sanctuary. That, or a reading nook for the ages.

______________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________

This address also comes complete with a detached garage off the laneway, a rare find for the area.

And speaking of the neighbourhood: beyond the craftsmanship, a key part of this home’s charm is its location — literal steps from the Queen West strip, calling 13 Euclid home would mean coffee at White Squirrel followed by a walk in the park as a daily routine. Sud Forno sandwiches would probably beckon most days, too. But we wouldn’t mind.
